opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly my thinking has shifted quite a bit. Early on, I was fairly skeptical. When you're talking about a rare disease, by definition you might have a handful of cases per hundred thousand people, so even a resource like UK Biobank with half a million participants might only capture a few dozen patients with a given condition. My instinct was that you just couldn't get the statistical power you need to say anything meaningful.

What's changed for me is a better appreciation of the depth of these resources, not just their breadth. When you have genomic data, imaging, longitudinal health records, and lifestyle information all linked for the same individuals, even a small number of cases can be incredibly informative, especially when you can compare them against a very large, well-characterized background population. You can start to look for subtle patterns that precede diagnosis, or identify people who carry relevant variants but were never diagnosed, which is something you'd never see in a traditional clinic-based cohort.

The other big shift is the idea of combining resources. No single databank is going to be enough for many rare conditions, but when you can harmonize data across UK Biobank, All of Us, and other national and hospital-based cohorts, the numbers start to become workable. All of Us is also particularly valuable because it's deliberately enrolling more diverse populations, and some rare diseases look quite different, or are more prevalent, in groups that have historically been underrepresented in research.

So I'd say I've gone from "probably not enough" to "not enough on its own, but surprisingly powerful when used thoughtfully and in combination." The challenge now is less about whether the information is there and more about building the methods, the machine learning approaches, and the data-sharing infrastructure to really make use of it while protecting patient privacy, which matters even more when you're dealing with very small, potentially identifiable groups.

r001.rationale: The response mentions longitudinal health records and patterns that may precede diagnosis, but does not clearly describe following initially disease-free participants as they develop disease.

r002.rationale: It says small case numbers can be informative and that databanks become workable when harmonized, concluding they are “surprisingly powerful” when used in combination.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say my thinking has moved from "no, almost by definition" to "it depends on what you mean by study, and what you're willing to borrow."

The early skepticism was simple arithmetic. A disease that affects one in fifty thousand people shows up maybe ten times in a cohort of half a million. You can't build a classifier on ten patients. You can't do a meaningful association study. So for a long time I treated these resources as useful for common disease and basically irrelevant for rare disease, and I think a lot of us did.

A few things changed that for me.

First, the imaging and multi-omic layers matured. UK Biobank now has tens of thousands of whole-body MRIs, cardiac scans, brain scans, plus proteomics and whole-genome sequencing on most participants. That shifted the question. You're no longer asking "how many people have this rare condition?" You're asking "what does normal look like at scale, with enormous precision?" And it turns out that is exactly what you need for rare disease. The hard part of rare disease has never been describing the patients. Clinicians at specialty centers know their patients intimately. The hard part is knowing how far outside normal they actually are, across organs, across ages, across ancestries. A biobank gives you that reference distribution. So the value is in the denominator, not the numerator.

Second, the rare disease world is increasingly organized around mechanism rather than diagnosis. Many rare conditions are extreme points on pathways that are perturbed mildly in common disease. If you have half a million people with genotypes and quantitative phenotypes, you can study the pathway even when you can't study the disease. Carriers of a pathogenic variant who never got a diagnosis are sitting in those cohorts, and they tell you about penetrance and about the early, subclinical picture that nobody sees in a clinic because people only show up once they're sick.

Third, and this is where my own work sits, the methods changed. Foundation models trained on large imaging cohorts let you learn representations from the common population and then adapt them with very few examples. Ten patients is hopeless from scratch. Ten patients on top of a model that already understands anatomy is a real study. So the biobank isn't where you find the rare patients, it's where you learn the prior that makes the rare patients analyzable.

What hasn't changed is my worry about who is in these cohorts. UK Biobank skews older, healthier, wealthier, and whiter than the UK itself. All of Us was explicitly designed to correct that, and it's doing better, but the normal you learn from a biased cohort is a biased normal. For rare disease that matters more, not less, because you're often making a judgment about one person based on where they fall relative to a reference. If the reference doesn't include people who look like them, you're going to misread them.

And I'd add one honest limit. Biobanks are terrible at the thing rare disease families care about most, which is longitudinal natural history. They were built as snapshots. The linkage to health records helps, but it's coarse. For that you still need the disease registries and the patient advocacy groups who have been quietly collecting data for decades. The right model isn't biobanks replacing those, it's the biobank as the reference and the registry as the signal, and we're only just getting good at putting the two together.

So the short version is: the databanks don't contain the rare disease. But they contain almost everything you need to understand it, as long as you stop looking for the patients and start looking for the context.

r001.rationale: The response says biobanks are poor for longitudinal natural history and does not describe following disease-free participants as they develop disease to identify signals.

r002.rationale: The response says biobanks can support rare-disease pathway studies and analyses that adapt large-cohort models with few patient examples, despite containing few rare-disease patients.

astra-6.text:
I’ve become more cautious about what “enough information” means. A databank can include a huge number of people, but when you focus on a particular rare disease, you may still have very few cases. And those cases may not have the detailed clinical information you need to understand how the disease develops or why patients have different outcomes.

So I’d distinguish between having enough data to discover a signal and having enough to understand a disease. Resources like UK Biobank and All of Us can be valuable starting points, but scale alone doesn’t settle the question. You also need the right measurements, reliable diagnoses, and information collected over time.

r001.rationale: The response mentions collecting information over time, but does not describe following initially disease-free participants as they develop disease or identifying signals from that longitudinal data.

r002.rationale: It calls the databanks valuable starting points but does not say they contain enough information for any rare-disease analyses; it emphasizes that case numbers and data quality may be inadequate.

sol-6.1.text:
I’ve become more cautious about what “enough information” means. A databank can be enormous and still have very few people with a particular rare disease. And even when those people are represented, the data may not capture the details you need—their symptoms over time, how the diagnosis was established, or their response to treatment.

So I’d distinguish between having enough data to find a signal and having enough to understand a disease. Resources like UK Biobank and All of Us can be valuable starting points, but the question is whether they contain the right patients and the right measurements for the question you’re asking. For rare diseases, that can mean connecting those broad resources with more detailed, disease-specific data.

r001.rationale: The response mentions data collected over time but does not describe following initially disease-free participants as they develop disease to identify signals.

r002.rationale: It calls the databanks valuable starting points and discusses finding signals, but does not clearly state that UK Biobank or All of Us contain enough information for at least some rare-disease analyses.
